rows.name: neutral_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination
rows.claim: The local incident energy flux is defined by:; where [equation] is the incident neutral energy flux attributed to recombination, [equation] is the cumulative incoming energy attributed to that channel, [equation] is wall area, and [equation] is time.; The subscript [equation] denotes the neutral channel; the superscripts [equation] and [equation] denote incidence and recombination attribution.; The quantity applies to incoming neutral particles carrying recombination-associated energy and is summed over neutral species and internal states, with neither resolution retained.; It is a local flux, not a wall-integrated power, and excludes ion-carried and radiative contributions, as well as outgoing neutral energy.; It is not the total kinetic-energy flux of all incident neutrals; only the recombination-attributed contribution is represented.; This is the energy-weighted counterpart of incident neutral particle flux at the wall due to recombination, which counts the incoming particles in the same channel without weighting by their carried energy.; It is directionally distinct from neutral particle flux at the wall due to recombination, which describes outgoing neutral products, and is restricted to recombination attribution unlike neutral energy flux at the wall.; This neutral-carried incident contribution is part of the broader energy flux at the wall due to recombination, which covers incident and outgoing contributions without selecting a direction; incident ion energy flux at the wall due to recombination describes the corresponding ion-carried incident channel.; Sign convention: Positive when neutral particles carrying recombination-associated energy cross the plasma-facing surface from the plasma-facing volume toward the material.

rows.name: contradicts-189
rows.planted_sentence: The back-surface distance reaches a conductor in front of the antenna strap.

item.documentation:
This quantity is the geometric standoff between the rear surface of an ion-cyclotron heating antenna strap and the conducting wall or other conductor located behind that surface.

The clearance is the shortest separation between the two relevant surfaces:

$$
d_{back} = \min_{\mathbf{r}_b \in S_b,\,\mathbf{r}_c \in S_c} \left\|\mathbf{r}_c - \mathbf{r}_b\right\|
$$

where $d_{\rm back}$ is the rear-surface clearance, $S_b$ is the strap back surface, $S_c$ is the facing conducting-wall or conductor surface, and $\mathbf{r}_b$ and $\mathbf{r}_c$ are position vectors on those surfaces.

The quantity applies only to the rear-facing separation of the antenna strap and does not denote the strap thickness, the distance to its inner or outer cylindrical boundaries, or either oblique cross-sectional length. The related [inner radius of the antenna strap](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), [outer radius of the antenna strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), [major length of the antenna strap](name:major_length_of_antenna_strap), and [minor length of the antenna strap](name:minor_length_of_antenna_strap) describe other strap dimensions rather than this conductor clearance.

This geometric clearance is an antenna-design parameter that influences the strap's loading resistance and radio-frequency coupling efficiency to the plasma; it is not itself an electrical resistance, coupling coefficient, or power quantity.

The back-surface distance reaches a conductor in front of the antenna strap.

rows.name: contradicts-264
rows.planted_sentence: The antenna-strap width is measured in the poloidal direction instead of the toroidal direction.

item.documentation:
Full toroidal width of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the edge-to-edge extent between the two toroidally separated sides of the strap conductor.

For a strap represented at a characteristic major radius, the toroidal width is related to the angular separation of the two toroidal edges by:

$$
w_\phi = R_\mathrm{strap}\,\Delta\phi
$$

where $w_\phi$ is the toroidal width, $R_\mathrm{strap}$ is the representative major radius of the strap, and $\Delta\phi$ is the smaller non-wrapping angular separation between the two toroidal edges.

This is a full width, not a half-width or a signed coordinate difference. It is distinct from the poloidal extent [height_of_antenna_strap](name:height_of_antenna_strap) and from the local-normal extent [thickness_of_antenna_strap](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the same strap conductor.

The antenna-strap width is measured in the poloidal direction instead of the toroidal direction.

rows.name: contradicts-242
rows.planted_sentence: The second local curvature radius is in the X1 direction instead of X2.

item.documentation:
Second local tangential (X2) back-surface radius of curvature of an optical element is the signed directional radius of curvature of the element's back surface in the surface-normal section whose tangent is the second object-local tangential direction. It characterizes the local surface figure of that back face when the back surface is curved.

The directional radius is the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature in the same surface direction:

$$
R_{2,\mathrm{back}} = \frac{1}{\kappa_{2,\mathrm{back}}}
$$

where $R_{2,\mathrm{back}}$ is the second local tangential back-surface radius of curvature of the optical element and $\kappa_{2,\mathrm{back}}$ is the signed normal curvature of the optical-element back surface in the same second object-local tangential direction.

The quantity applies to one optical element and to its back surface only. It is defined only for curved back-surface types for which a second local tangential radius is specified; it is not a planar-surface parameter, not an average over surfaces, optical elements, or tangential directions, and not a radius along any machine-fixed axis.

The [first local tangential back-surface radius of an optical element](name:first_local_tangential_back_surface_radius_of_optical_element) is the corresponding radius on the same back surface along the orthogonal first object-local tangential direction. The [second local tangential front-surface radius of an optical element](name:second_local_tangential_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element) is the opposite-surface counterpart along the same second object-local tangential direction. In optical-element surface names that use vertical for this surface direction, such as [vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) and [vertical front-surface radius of an optical element](name:vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element), vertical denotes the same object-local second tangential direction, not a machine-fixed direction.

Sign convention: Positive when the center of curvature of the back-surface normal section in the second local tangential direction lies in the direction of the oriented local normal of the back surface.

The second local curvature radius is in the X1 direction instead of X2.

rows.name: contradicts-429
rows.planted_sentence: Relative humidity is measured at the radiation source instead of the detector.

item.documentation:
Relative humidity at the detector is the ambient water-vapor content expressed relative to the maximum water-vapor content supported at the local air temperature.

It is defined by

$$
RH = \frac{p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}{p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)}
$$

where $RH$ is relative humidity, $p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ is the partial pressure of water vapor surrounding the detector, $p_{\mathrm{sat}}(T)$ is the saturation vapor pressure of water, and $T$ is the local air temperature. The reported fraction is bounded from 0 to 1.

This quantity describes the environmental moisture condition at the detector and is not absolute humidity, air temperature, or a detector-response property. It is distinct from an intrinsic detection metric such as [spectral efficiency of a hard X-ray detector](name:spectral_efficiency_of_hard_xray_detector), which describes photon-registration probability rather than the surrounding environment.

Relative humidity is measured at the radiation source instead of the detector.

rows.name: contradicts-51
rows.planted_sentence: Conducted power includes only one divertor target and excludes the others.

item.documentation:
The power of the divertor due to conduction is the total thermal energy deposited on all divertor target surfaces by electron and ion heat conduction along open scrape-off-layer magnetic field lines. It excludes convective particle enthalpy, absorbed radiation, recombination, and neutral-particle contributions, and is the divertor-wide counterpart of [power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction).

The total conductive power is defined by integrating the conductive heat-flux vector over every wetted divertor target surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{div,cond}} = \sum_k \int_{A_k} \mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cond}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_k\,dA
$$

where $A_k$ is the wetted surface of target $k$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_k$ points from the plasma toward the target material, and $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the sum of the electron and ion conductive heat-flux vectors. This aggregate quantity covers the complete divertor assembly and is a locus-specific component of [power_due_to_conduction](name:power_due_to_conduction), rather than the global wall quantity [power_at_wall_due_to_conduction](name:power_at_wall_due_to_conduction).

Conducted power includes only one divertor target and excludes the others.

rows.name: contradicts-404
rows.planted_sentence: Radiated power includes only one divertor target and excludes the others.

item.documentation:
This quantity is the total thermal radiative power emitted by the surfaces of all divertor targets. It represents surface emission governed by the local surface temperature and emissivity.

$$
P_{\mathrm{bb}} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{D}} \int_{A_i} \epsilon_i\,\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}\,T_i^4\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the emitted thermal radiative power, $\mathcal{D}$ is the set of divertor target surfaces, $A_i$ is the surface area of target $i$, $\epsilon_i$ is its local thermal emissivity, $\sigma_{\mathrm{SB}}$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, $T_i$ is its local absolute surface temperature, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element.

The quantity is aggregated over every divertor target surface and includes emissivity effects. It describes radiation emitted by the targets, not plasma power incident on them or radiation retained after reflection.

It is distinct from [absorbed radiated power of the divertor](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_divertor), which is the net radiative power deposited on the targets after accounting for incident and reflected radiation, and from [total incident power of the divertor](name:total_incident_power_of_divertor), which describes incoming plasma power rather than surface emission.

Radiated power includes only one divertor target and excludes the others.

rows.name: contradicts-35
rows.planted_sentence: The beam power is launched out of the vacuum vessel.

item.documentation:
Launched power is the electromagnetic power carried by one specified electron-cyclotron beam into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma. It represents injected beam power rather than energy deposited in the plasma.

The power is defined as the rate of electromagnetic energy transport:

$$
P_{\mathrm{launched}} = \frac{dE}{dt}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{launched}}$ is the launched beam power, $E$ is the electromagnetic energy transported by the beam, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to an individual electron-cyclotron beam and is not an aggregate over multiple beams or a complete launcher system. Transmission losses before launch are excluded from the launched value; plasma absorption and power reflected after launch are also excluded.

The beam's carrier frequency, represented by the [electron-cyclotron beam frequency](name:frequency_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), determines its cyclotron-resonance condition, while launched power specifies the strength of the injected electromagnetic beam.

The beam power is launched out of the vacuum vessel.

rows.name: contradicts-273
rows.planted_sentence: Bandwidth is the center frequency of the intermediate-frequency bandpass rather than its full width.

item.documentation:
The bandwidth is the total frequency span passed by the intermediate-frequency bandpass filter associated with one electron-cyclotron-emission radiometer channel. It characterizes the channel's accepted spectral interval rather than an emission intensity or a plasma frequency.

The full width is defined by

$$
\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}} = f_{\mathrm{high}} - f_{\mathrm{low}}
$$

where $\Delta f_{\mathrm{IF}}$ is the intermediate-frequency bandwidth, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ is the upper bandpass edge frequency, and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ is the lower bandpass edge frequency.

This quantity applies to one ECE channel and uses the full-width convention; it is not the center frequency, a reference carrier frequency, or a wavelength-domain response width such as the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). The accepted interval determines which electron-cyclotron-emission frequencies contribute to the [radiative temperature at an ECE channel](name:radiative_temperature_at_ece_channel) and can therefore affect the channel's effective radial localization.

Bandwidth is the center frequency of the intermediate-frequency bandpass rather than its full width.

rows.name: contradicts-250
rows.planted_sentence: Line-averaged density multiplies the line integral by the line-of-sight length.

item.documentation:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume averaged along a complete propagation chord is the path-normalized continuum count density of the unqualified free-electron population along that chord.

For local [electron density](name:electron_density) $n_e(l)$, the defining relation is:

$$
\bar{n}_e = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_e(l)\,dl
$$

where $\bar{n}_e$ is the line-averaged electron density, $n_e(l)$ is the local free-electron density at path coordinate $l$, $l$ is distance along the complete propagation chord, and $L$ is the full chord length.

This quantity applies to the complete unqualified free-electron population along the chord, aggregating all contributing free-electron populations rather than selecting thermal or fast electrons. It is a path average over the chord and is not a pointwise [electron density](name:electron_density) or a line-integrated column density.

The numerator in the defining relation is the [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density); dividing it by the chord length produces this path-normalized quantity. The same line-averaging construction applies to species-specific quantities such as [line-averaged hydrogen density](name:line_averaged_hydrogen_density), while this quantity remains specific to free electrons.

Line-averaged density multiplies the line integral by the line-of-sight length.

rows.name: contradicts-12
rows.planted_sentence: The squareness describes the lower inner plasma boundary.

item.documentation:
The upper-inner squareness of the plasma boundary is the dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying the departure of the upper inboard corner of the last closed flux surface from a reference ellipse. It is the upper-quadrant component of the [inner squareness of the plasma boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), paired with the [lower-inner squareness of the plasma boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary).

In a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the coefficient is

$$
\zeta_{\mathrm{UI}} = \frac{\overline{OD} - \overline{OE}}{\overline{OF} - \overline{OE}}
$$

where $O$ is the reference-ellipse center, $D$ is the upper-inner boundary intersection along the corner diagonal, $E$ is the corresponding ellipse intersection, and $F$ is the corner of the circumscribing rectangle. The reference ellipse is determined by the boundary size and shaping parameters.

The squareness describes the lower inner plasma boundary.

rows.name: contradicts-476
rows.planted_sentence: Roughness zero is perfectly rough and one is perfectly specular.

item.documentation:
Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies how the element partitions reflected radiation between a specular component and a diffuse component. The endpoint value zero denotes ideal specular reflection, and the endpoint value one denotes ideal diffuse reflection.

The parameter is defined from the reflected-power partition as

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{spec}} + P_{\mathrm{diff}}, \qquad r = \frac{P_{\mathrm{diff}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{spec}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}}, \qquad 0 \le r \le 1
$$

where $r$ is the roughness parameter, and $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{spec}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{diff}}$ are radiant powers in watts for the total reflected, ideal-specular, and diffuse reflected components under the same incident radiation and optical state.

This quantity is not a metrological surface-height roughness such as an rms height or correlation length. item.documentation:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar coefficient for Fickian diffusion of runaway electrons perpendicular to the magnetic field. rows.name: contradicts-311
rows.planted_sentence: Normalized pressure subtracts perpendicular pressure from parallel pressure.

item.documentation:
Normalized perturbed pressure Bessel-1 is the dimensionless total pressure response of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, formed from parallel and perpendicular pressure moments weighted by the first-order Bessel function evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument and normalized to the equilibrium species pressure. It is a species-resolved complex amplitude representing the finite-Larmor-radius part of the gyrocenter pressure response.

For species $s$, it is defined by the sum of the first-order Bessel-weighted parallel and perpendicular pressure moments divided by the equilibrium species pressure:

$$
\widehat{P}^{(J_1)}_s = \frac{P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} + P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}}{p_s}, \qquad P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s v_\parallel^2 J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}, \qquad P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s \frac{v_\perp^2}{2} J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}
$$

where $P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)}$ and $P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}$ are pressure-moment amplitudes with pressure units, $p_s=n_sT_s$ is the equilibrium species pressure when $T_s$ is expressed as energy per particle, $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are velocities parallel and perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the perturbation amplitude of the gyrocenter distribution. The first-order Bessel function $J_1$ is evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument $\lambda_s=k_\perp v_\perp/\Omega_s$, with $k_\perp$ the magnitude of the wave vector perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field and $\Omega_s=|q_s|B/m_s$ the positive cyclotron-frequency magnitude.

The total moment is the sum of parallel_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1 and [perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1](name:perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1). It is a gyrocenter-distribution moment with explicit $J_1(\lambda_s)$ weighting; it is distinct from normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure, which lacks this Bessel-1 weighting, and from particle-distribution pressure perturbations such as normalized_perturbed_pressure and normalized_total_particle_perturbed_pressure_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode. Because $J_1(0)=0$, this member vanishes at zero gyroaveraging argument.

In a linear eigenmode, $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the complex coefficient multiplying the chosen harmonic phase factor. This moment inherits the same arbitrary global amplitude and phase normalization as the eigenmode; changing the reference phase multiplies all perturbation amplitudes by the same complex factor, so its sign and phase are defined only relative to that reference.

rows.name: contradicts-191
rows.planted_sentence: The angle concerns particles emitted from the wall rather than the incident species.

item.documentation:
Incident angle at wall is the geometrical angle between the velocity direction of an incident neutral particle at impact and the local wall-surface normal directed from the plasma-facing side into the wall material. It characterizes the incidence direction of a selected neutral-particle species on the wall.

The incidence angle $\alpha$ is defined by

$$
\alpha = \arccos\left(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}\right)
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}$ is the unit direction of the incoming neutral-particle velocity at the impact point and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}$ is the local wall-surface unit normal directed into the wall material.

The scope is a specified neutral incident species interacting with the wall. The allowed interval is $0 \le \alpha \le \pi/2$: $\alpha=0$ corresponds to normal incidence into the wall, and $\alpha=\pi/2$ corresponds to tangential grazing incidence. Directions for which the particle is leaving the wall-facing half-space are not incident angles.

This quantity is the angular argument for the physical sputtering dependence of that neutral species at the wall. It is not the physical sputtering coefficient, not an angle for emitted or sputtered particles, and not an average over neutral species or wall locations.

rows.name: contradicts-372
rows.planted_sentence: This is total launched wave power before absorption.

item.documentation:
Total absorbed wave power is the total rate at which coherent electromagnetic waves transfer energy directly to all plasma particle populations, with contributions integrated over the plasma volume.

$$
P_{\rm abs} = \left.\frac{dE_{\rm particles}}{dt}\right|_{\rm waves}
$$

where $P_{\rm abs}$ is absorbed wave power, $E_{\rm particles}$ is the combined energy of all included plasma particle populations, $t$ is time, and the subscript “waves” restricts the derivative to direct energy transfer from the coherent electromagnetic-wave field.

This quantity is globally aggregated: it is summed over all species, charge states, populations, and spatial locations. It includes direct wave-to-particle transfer and excludes electromagnetic power that remains in the wave field and energy subsequently redistributed between particle populations by collisions.

It is the species-summed specialization of [absorbed wave power](name:absorbed_wave_power), unlike [electron absorbed wave power](name:electron_absorbed_wave_power), which is restricted to electron populations. It is also the global counterpart of [total absorbed wave power at the inside flux surface](name:total_absorbed_wave_power_at_inside_flux_surface), which retains only the power enclosed within a selected flux surface; Fourier-resolved contributions are represented by [per-toroidal-mode total absorbed wave power](name:per_toroidal_mode_total_absorbed_wave_power).

rows.name: contradicts-471
rows.planted_sentence: Thermal-electron power inside a flux surface is only the local density at that surface.

item.documentation:
Thermal electron power at an inside flux surface quantifies the total rate at which coherent wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume bounded by a given magnetic flux surface. It is the thermal-electron contribution to [electron power at an inside flux surface](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), distinct from the suprathermal contribution [fast electron power at an inside flux surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The quantity is obtained by integrating the flux-surface-averaged thermal-electron power density $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho') \frac{dV}{d\rho'} \, d\rho'
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho)$ is the cumulative absorbed power, $\rho$ labels the limiting magnetic flux surface, $\rho'$ is the integration variable, $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ is the local thermal-electron absorbed power density, and $dV/d\rho'$ is the differential enclosed volume per unit flux-surface label. Only absorption by bulk thermal electrons is included; fast-electron and ion absorption, launched power, and absorption outside the enclosed volume are excluded. At the outermost closed flux surface, it gives the total wave power absorbed by thermal electrons.

rows.planted_sentence: Flux expansion is strike-point poloidal field divided by midplane-separatrix poloidal field.

item.documentation:
Magnetic flux expansion compares the poloidal magnetic-field strength upstream of the divertor with that at the downstream strike point. It quantifies the widening of a magnetic flux tube as it connects the upstream separatrix to the divertor target.

$$

$$

This is a global characteristic time based on the plasma minor radius and applies to resistive current diffusion and resistive magnetohydrodynamic evolution. It is not a local diffusion time, a mode growth time, or an instantaneous current value.

The timescale increases with the square of the minor radius and decreases as neoclassical resistivity increases; it therefore reflects the plasma electrical conductivity and the evolution rate of the current distribution.

item.documentation:
The deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DT}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-T fusion reactions. Each D-T fusion reaction produces exactly one neutron, so this quantity is equal to the local D-T fusion reaction-rate density.

For reacting deuterium and tritium ion populations, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity, the velocity-averaged fusion cross-section evaluated over the relative-velocity distribution of the reacting ion populations; for thermal reactants it is the thermally averaged reactivity at the local ion temperature. No symmetry factor appears because the reactants are distinct species.

This quantity counts neutron production, not fusion energy deposition or neutron power. It is the D-T channel of the parent emissivity_due_to_fusion and the counterpart of [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which covers the neutron-emitting D-D branch. rows.name: contradicts-35

item.documentation:
Launched power is the electromagnetic power carried by one specified electron-cyclotron beam into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma. It represents injected beam power rather than energy deposited in the plasma.

$$

rows.planted_sentence: The toroidal angle grows clockwise when viewed from above.

item.documentation:
Toroidal angle of a coil-conductor element is the azimuthal coordinate $\phi$ of a specified geometric locus on a conductor element about the toroidal symmetry axis. It is the angular coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\phi=0$ is the chosen radial half-plane.

For the same locus represented in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and $+\hat{x}$ lying in the $\phi=0$ half-plane, the principal angular representative is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x)

item.documentation:
Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies how the element partitions reflected radiation between a specular component and a diffuse component. The endpoint value zero denotes ideal specular reflection, and the endpoint value one denotes ideal diffuse reflection.

The parameter is defined from the reflected-power partition as

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{spec}} + P_{\mathrm{diff}}, \qquad r = \frac{P_{\mathrm{diff}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{spec}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}}, \qquad 0 \le r \le 1
$$

where $r$ is the roughness parameter, and $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{spec}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{diff}}$ are radiant powers in watts for the total reflected, ideal-specular, and diffuse reflected components under the same incident radiation and optical state.

This quantity is not a metrological surface-height roughness such as an rms height or correlation length. Intermediate values specify the diffuse fraction of reflected power in the stated partition; they do not by themselves prescribe the angular distribution of the diffuse component, require Lambertian scattering, or include transmitted or absorbed power.

Electrical resistance of a discrete passive-conductor element is the proportionality between the voltage drop across the element and the current through it, representing irreversible ohmic dissipation.

$$

where $R$ is the resistance, $\Delta V$ is the potential difference across the element, and $I$ is the through-current. For an approximately homogeneous element, resistance is determined by the material resistivity and the element geometry, as described by [resistivity of the vacuum vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) and [resistivity of wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). This lumped quantity excludes inductive opposition and represents only the ohmic component; it is distinct from the total resistance of a closed [passive loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop).

$$
TBR_{\mathrm{module}} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{module}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{module}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in the module's breeding regions and $N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}$ is the incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.

For modules that partition the blanket breeding regions and share this denominator, the module contributions add to the blanket tritium breeding ratio. The quantity excludes tritium production outside the specified module and is not a separate normalization of the module's incident neutron count.

rows.name: contradicts-30
rows.planted_sentence: Atomic number denotes nuclear mass instead of nuclear charge.

item.documentation:
Atomic number identifies an element through the number of protons in its nucleus. It is an intrinsic element identifier that remains unchanged when the element is bound in a molecule or changes ionization state.

The atomic number $Z$ is defined by

$$
Z = N_p
$$

where $N_p$ is the number of protons in the element's nucleus.

This quantity applies to the selected element constituent of a neutral or charged species, including an element within a compound or molecule. It identifies one element and is not summed over constituent elements, isotopes, or charge states.

Atomic number is distinct from [ion charge](name:ion_charge), which describes the net electric charge of an ion and may change while $Z$ remains fixed. Unlike [fast ion atomic number](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), this generic identifier carries no fixed fast-ion role or diagnostic context.

rows.name: contradicts-133
rows.planted_sentence: The quantity is a source rate for fast-particle density rather than thermal particle density.

item.documentation:
Co-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the co-passing orbit class. Co-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is in the plasma-current direction.

The net source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \left\langle s_{n,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{co,th}} - s_{n,\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{co,th}} \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the co-passing thermal particle source rate, $s_{n,\mathrm{in}}^{\mathrm{co,th}}$ is the local rate of thermal-particle addition, $s_{n,\mathrm{out}}^{\mathrm{co,th}}$ is the local rate of thermal-particle removal, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes averaging over a magnetic flux surface, and $\psi$ is the magnetic-flux label of that surface.

The quantity applies only to the thermal population on co-passing, untrapped passing orbits and is aggregated by flux-surface averaging. Positive values represent a net source to this orbit class, while negative values represent a net sink. It excludes trapped and counter-passing orbit populations and describes particle-number transfer rather than energy or momentum transfer.

This is one orbit-class contribution to the broader [thermal particle source rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate), which aggregates source and sink contributions over the thermal orbit populations. The [counter-passing thermal particle source rate](name:counter_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) is the corresponding orbit-class contribution for particles circulating opposite to the plasma-current direction.

The quantity is a source rate for fast-particle density rather than thermal particle density.

rows.name: contradicts-380
rows.planted_sentence: This quantity is a convective velocity rather than an effective diffusivity.

item.documentation:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar coefficient for Fickian diffusion of runaway electrons perpendicular to the magnetic field. In flux-surface transport descriptions, it represents the cross-surface diffusive transport component along the flux-surface normal, positive toward increasing flux label.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial \ell_\perp}
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive part of the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux), $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway-electron density](name:runaway_electron_density), and $\ell_\perp$ is distance along the local flux-surface-normal direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. The minus sign states that a positive diffusivity gives diffusive flux from larger toward smaller runaway-electron density.

This quantity applies only to the runaway-electron population and only to its perpendicular diffusive particle transport. It is not a parallel transport coefficient, not a convective velocity, and not the full [runaway-electron diffusivity](name:runaway_electron_diffusivity) when that broader quantity includes additional directional components.

The [perpendicular runaway-electron convection velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) gives the advective contribution to the same perpendicular particle balance, whereas $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ multiplies the density gradient. The sum of diffusive and convective contributions forms the modeled [perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

This quantity is a convective velocity rather than an effective diffusivity.

rows.name: contradicts-311
rows.planted_sentence: Normalized pressure subtracts perpendicular pressure from parallel pressure.

item.documentation:
Normalized perturbed pressure Bessel-1 is the dimensionless total pressure response of a perturbed gyrocenter distribution in a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode, formed from parallel and perpendicular pressure moments weighted by the first-order Bessel function evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument and normalized to the equilibrium species pressure. It is a species-resolved complex amplitude representing the finite-Larmor-radius part of the gyrocenter pressure response.

For species $s$, it is defined by the sum of the first-order Bessel-weighted parallel and perpendicular pressure moments divided by the equilibrium species pressure:

$$
\widehat{P}^{(J_1)}_s = \frac{P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} + P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}}{p_s}, \qquad P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s v_\parallel^2 J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}, \qquad P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)} = \int d^3v\, m_s \frac{v_\perp^2}{2} J_1(\lambda_s)\widetilde{F}_{g,s}
$$

where $P_{\parallel s}^{(J_1)}$ and $P_{\perp s}^{(J_1)}$ are pressure-moment amplitudes with pressure units, $p_s=n_sT_s$ is the equilibrium species pressure when $T_s$ is expressed as energy per particle, $m_s$ is the species mass, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are velocities parallel and perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, and $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the perturbation amplitude of the gyrocenter distribution. The first-order Bessel function $J_1$ is evaluated on the gyroaveraging argument $\lambda_s=k_\perp v_\perp/\Omega_s$, with $k_\perp$ the magnitude of the wave vector perpendicular to the equilibrium magnetic field and $\Omega_s=|q_s|B/m_s$ the positive cyclotron-frequency magnitude.

The total moment is the sum of parallel_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1 and [perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1](name:perpendicular_normalized_perturbed_pressure_bessel_1). It is a gyrocenter-distribution moment with explicit $J_1(\lambda_s)$ weighting; it is distinct from normalized_gyrocenter_perturbed_pressure, which lacks this Bessel-1 weighting, and from particle-distribution pressure perturbations such as normalized_perturbed_pressure and normalized_total_particle_perturbed_pressure_of_gyrokinetic_eigenmode. Because $J_1(0)=0$, this member vanishes at zero gyroaveraging argument.

In a linear eigenmode, $\widetilde{F}_{g,s}$ is the complex coefficient multiplying the chosen harmonic phase factor. This moment inherits the same arbitrary global amplitude and phase normalization as the eigenmode; changing the reference phase multiplies all perturbation amplitudes by the same complex factor, so its sign and phase are defined only relative to that reference.

Normalized pressure subtracts perpendicular pressure from parallel pressure.

rows.name: contradicts-191
rows.planted_sentence: The angle concerns particles emitted from the wall rather than the incident species.

item.documentation:
Incident angle at wall is the geometrical angle between the velocity direction of an incident neutral particle at impact and the local wall-surface normal directed from the plasma-facing side into the wall material. It characterizes the incidence direction of a selected neutral-particle species on the wall.

The incidence angle $\alpha$ is defined by

$$
\alpha = \arccos\left(\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}\right)
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{v}}_\mathrm{inc}$ is the unit direction of the incoming neutral-particle velocity at the impact point and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{in}$ is the local wall-surface unit normal directed into the wall material.

The scope is a specified neutral incident species interacting with the wall. The allowed interval is $0 \le \alpha \le \pi/2$: $\alpha=0$ corresponds to normal incidence into the wall, and $\alpha=\pi/2$ corresponds to tangential grazing incidence. Directions for which the particle is leaving the wall-facing half-space are not incident angles.

This quantity is the angular argument for the physical sputtering dependence of that neutral species at the wall. It is not the physical sputtering coefficient, not an angle for emitted or sputtered particles, and not an average over neutral species or wall locations.

The angle concerns particles emitted from the wall rather than the incident species.

rows.name: contradicts-372
rows.planted_sentence: This is total launched wave power before absorption.

item.documentation:
Total absorbed wave power is the total rate at which coherent electromagnetic waves transfer energy directly to all plasma particle populations, with contributions integrated over the plasma volume.

$$
P_{\rm abs} = \left.\frac{dE_{\rm particles}}{dt}\right|_{\rm waves}
$$

where $P_{\rm abs}$ is absorbed wave power, $E_{\rm particles}$ is the combined energy of all included plasma particle populations, $t$ is time, and the subscript “waves” restricts the derivative to direct energy transfer from the coherent electromagnetic-wave field.

This quantity is globally aggregated: it is summed over all species, charge states, populations, and spatial locations. It includes direct wave-to-particle transfer and excludes electromagnetic power that remains in the wave field and energy subsequently redistributed between particle populations by collisions.

It is the species-summed specialization of [absorbed wave power](name:absorbed_wave_power), unlike [electron absorbed wave power](name:electron_absorbed_wave_power), which is restricted to electron populations. It is also the global counterpart of [total absorbed wave power at the inside flux surface](name:total_absorbed_wave_power_at_inside_flux_surface), which retains only the power enclosed within a selected flux surface; Fourier-resolved contributions are represented by [per-toroidal-mode total absorbed wave power](name:per_toroidal_mode_total_absorbed_wave_power).

This is total launched wave power before absorption.

rows.name: contradicts-471
rows.planted_sentence: Thermal-electron power inside a flux surface is only the local density at that surface.

item.documentation:
Thermal electron power at an inside flux surface quantifies the total rate at which coherent wave energy is absorbed by the bulk thermal electron population within the plasma volume bounded by a given magnetic flux surface. It is the thermal-electron contribution to [electron power at an inside flux surface](name:electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), distinct from the suprathermal contribution [fast electron power at an inside flux surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface).

The quantity is obtained by integrating the flux-surface-averaged thermal-electron power density $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ over the enclosed plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho) = \int_0^\rho p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho') \frac{dV}{d\rho'} \, d\rho'
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}(\rho)$ is the cumulative absorbed power, $\rho$ labels the limiting magnetic flux surface, $\rho'$ is the integration variable, $p_{\mathrm{thermal,e}}$ is the local thermal-electron absorbed power density, and $dV/d\rho'$ is the differential enclosed volume per unit flux-surface label. Only absorption by bulk thermal electrons is included; fast-electron and ion absorption, launched power, and absorption outside the enclosed volume are excluded. At the outermost closed flux surface, it gives the total wave power absorbed by thermal electrons.

Thermal-electron power inside a flux surface is only the local density at that surface.

item.documentation:
Normal non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the signed component of the toroidally varying external-coil vacuum magnetic field normal to a generic control surface. It is a scalar projection evaluated at points on that surface, rather than the full magnetic-field vector.

The defining projection is

$$
B_n(R,\phi,Z)=\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}(R,\phi,Z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}(R,\phi,Z)
$$

where $B_n$ is the normal magnetic-field component, $\mathbf{B}_{\rm NA}$ is the [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the oriented unit normal to the control surface. The coordinates $R$, $\phi$, and $Z$ are major radius, toroidal angle, and vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

This quantity applies to the external-coil vacuum contribution at each selected point of a generic control surface, which is not assumed to be a magnetic flux surface. Its aggregation convention is the inherited removal of the toroidal-angle average from the vacuum field; no surface or area average is implied.

It excludes the toroidally symmetric vacuum field and magnetic-field contributions generated by plasma currents. It also excludes tangential components and is distinct from cylindrical projections such as the [vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field); the normal direction is defined by the control surface rather than by the cylindrical basis.

The scalar $B_n$ is the surface-normal component of the vector [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field). Reversing the assigned orientation of the control-surface normal reverses $B_n$, while the parent vector itself is unchanged.

rows.name: contradicts-358
rows.planted_sentence: Flux expansion is strike-point poloidal field divided by midplane-separatrix poloidal field.

item.documentation:
Magnetic flux expansion compares the poloidal magnetic-field strength upstream of the divertor with that at the downstream strike point. It quantifies the widening of a magnetic flux tube as it connects the upstream separatrix to the divertor target.

$$
F_x = \frac{B_{p,u}}{B_{p,t}}
$$

where $F_x$ is the magnetic flux-expansion factor, $B_{p,u}$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field at the outboard midplane separatrix, and $B_{p,t}$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field at the strike point.

The quantity is a local ratio for the specified upstream and target locations; it is not summed or averaged over flux surfaces, divertor targets, or strike points. It uses the poloidal-field magnitude rather than the total magnetic-field magnitude or a single cylindrical component. The strike-point location is the geometric point whose major-radius position is described by the [radial coordinate of the strike point](name:radial_coordinate_of_strike_point).

A larger $F_x$ indicates greater magnetic spreading between the upstream separatrix and the target, allowing a given parallel heat flow to be distributed over a wider wetted target area.

rows.name: contradicts-107
rows.planted_sentence: Inverse phase-ellipse curvature is negative for divergent beams and positive for convergent beams.

item.documentation:
Wave curvature of an electron-cyclotron beam is the signed curvature of the beam phase front resolved along one selected principal transverse direction of the phase ellipse. It is a scalar Gaussian-optics phase-front parameter for a single principal direction.

The selected scalar curvature is defined by the reciprocal of the corresponding signed curvature radius of the phase front:

$$
\kappa_i = \frac{1}{R_i}
$$

where $\kappa_i$ is the wave curvature of the electron-cyclotron beam resolved along selected principal transverse direction $i$, $R_i$ is the signed radius of curvature of the beam phase front along that direction, and $i$ identifies one of the two principal axes of the phase ellipse.

The quantity applies to an electron-cyclotron beam represented by a local Gaussian phase ellipse. It is defined only after one principal transverse direction $i$ has been selected; the selector may be the first or second principal phase-ellipse axis, or an explicitly defined beam-local horizontal or vertical axis when that naming convention is used. No averaging, summation, or magnitude over the two principal directions is implied.

The two scalar values obtained by selecting the two principal phase-ellipse axes are the principal curvatures of the local phase-front curvature tensor. This quantity is distinct from beam-envelope size, absolute wave phase, and beam propagation-angle quantities such as the [toroidal angle of the electron-cyclotron beam](name:toroidal_angle_of_electron_cyclotron_beam), which specify other aspects of the same beam rather than phase-front bending.

Sign convention: Positive when the beam phase front is divergent in the selected principal transverse direction as distance increases along the beam-propagation direction.

Inverse phase-ellipse curvature is negative for divergent beams and positive for convergent beams.

item.documentation:
This quantity is the additional lumped ohmic resistance introduced externally in the circuit of an individual poloidal-field coil. It represents resistance from added circuit elements such as dynamically switchable resistors, rather than the coil winding itself.

At a given time, the effective coil resistance is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{eff}} = R_{\mathrm{winding}} + R_{\mathrm{ext}}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the total effective resistance of the coil circuit, $R_{\mathrm{winding}}$ is the static winding resistance represented by [resistance of a poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $R_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is this additional external resistance.

The quantity applies to one poloidal-field coil and is a scalar lumped circuit property that may vary as the externally added resistance changes. It excludes the static winding resistance itself and does not denote an unrelated power-supply or Thevenin resistance. Its additive relationship to [resistance of a poloidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) distinguishes it from the baseline winding resistance; together they determine the coil circuit's effective ohmic opposition and resistive voltage drop.

Effective coil resistance subtracts the dynamic resistance from the static resistance.

rows.name: contradicts-125
rows.planted_sentence: This quantity is the fluid pressure at the port instead of its temperature.

item.documentation:
Coolant temperature is the thermodynamic temperature describing the thermal state of the working fluid at a connection port of a power-conversion component.

The quantity applies to coolant at a generic plant-component port, which may be an inlet or an outlet. It denotes the local fluid state at that port; no summation, spatial averaging, or integration is implied. It excludes the temperature of the component structure or any other material.

Unlike [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet), this quantity does not restrict the port to an outlet. It is a thermal-state quantity, whereas [coolant transit time of plant component port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) describes the elapsed transport time between component ports rather than the coolant temperature.

This quantity is the fluid pressure at the port instead of its temperature.

item.documentation:

For an ideal right circular cylindrical pellet, the diameter and axial length determine the pellet volume by

$$

$$

This quantity excludes the axial extent of the pellet, which is the [length of pellet](name:length_of_pellet), and excludes characteristic sizes of shattered fragments, ablated material, or the post-shattering material cloud.

The quantity is the pellet radius rather than its diameter.

rows.name: contradicts-62
rows.planted_sentence: The momentum-velocity component is perpendicular rather than parallel.

item.documentation:
Parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection is the scalar component, along the local magnetic-field direction, of an effective convection velocity for transport of momentum carried by a neutral population in one resolved internal state. It is a transport velocity for momentum, not the neutral bulk-flow velocity itself.

The scalar projection is defined by

$$
v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $v_{\parallel,\mathrm{eff}}$ is this parallel effective neutral internal-state momentum velocity due to convection, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the corresponding [neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection), and $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/\lvert\mathbf{B}\rvert$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

The scope is a single resolved neutral internal state, so no summation or averaging over internal states is implied. This quantity is the field-aligned component only; it excludes perpendicular components, particle-density convection velocities, energy convection velocities, diffusivities, and source terms. In a convective momentum-transport closure, it is the effective velocity factor associated with the transported neutral internal-state momentum.

Sign convention: Positive when the projection of the effective convection velocity is in the direction of the local magnetic field.

The momentum-velocity component is perpendicular rather than parallel.

rows.name: contradicts-399
rows.planted_sentence: The emissivity is due to deuterium-deuterium reactions instead of deuterium-tritium reactions.

item.documentation:
The deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DT}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-T fusion reactions. Each D-T fusion reaction produces exactly one neutron, so this quantity is equal to the local D-T fusion reaction-rate density.

For reacting deuterium and tritium ion populations, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity, the velocity-averaged fusion cross-section evaluated over the relative-velocity distribution of the reacting ion populations; for thermal reactants it is the thermally averaged reactivity at the local ion temperature. No symmetry factor appears because the reactants are distinct species.

This quantity counts neutron production, not fusion energy deposition or neutron power. It is the D-T channel of the parent emissivity_due_to_fusion and the counterpart of [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which covers the neutron-emitting D-D branch. Its energy-weighted counterpart is [deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion), and integrating the emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the per-reaction neutron energy connects to the total_neutron_power.

The emissivity is due to deuterium-deuterium reactions instead of deuterium-tritium reactions.

rows.name: contradicts-65
rows.planted_sentence: Marker weight counts markers represented by each real particle.

item.documentation:
This quantity is the statistical weight of one Monte Carlo particle marker: the number of real physical particles represented by that marker. It converts a discrete marker ensemble into the corresponding physical particle population.

$$
w = \frac{N_{\mathrm{real}}}{N_{\mathrm{sim}}}
$$

where $w$ is the marker weight, $N_{\mathrm{real}}$ is the represented real-particle count, and $N_{\mathrm{sim}}$ is the simulated-particle count associated with the marker. The weight is dimensionless and may be used to form macroscopic distribution moments by weighting marker contributions. It is the ratio-valued derivative of particle_simulated_count, while particle_count denotes the corresponding particle-count quantity rather than the marker weight itself.

rows.name: contradicts-169
rows.planted_sentence: The vorticity component is along the major-radius axis instead of the height axis.

item.documentation:
Vertical vorticity is the component of the plasma vorticity vector along the vertical direction. It measures the signed local rotation of the bulk plasma flow in the horizontal plane and is one directional projection of [vorticity](name:vorticity).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining relation is:

$$
\omega_Z = \boldsymbol{\omega}\cdot\hat{Z} = (\nabla\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the local bulk plasma velocity in m/s, $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ is the vorticity vector in s$^{-1}$, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector. Here $R$ is major radius in m, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in m.

The related [toroidal vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity) projects the same vorticity vector onto $\hat{\phi}$ instead. The major-radius-scaled quantity [vertical vorticity divided by major radius](name:ratio_of_vertical_vorticity_to_major_radius) is distinct because it includes an additional inverse-length factor.

Sign convention: Positive when the bulk velocity field rotates in the right-hand sense about the positive vertical direction $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The vorticity component is along the major-radius axis instead of the height axis.

rows.name: contradicts-450
rows.planted_sentence: This is an injected electron-equivalent particle flux instead of a pumped one.

item.documentation:
The rate at which particles of the electron-equivalent population are removed from the plasma region by wall pumping is the global scalar representation of the wall particle-removal flux. It describes pumped particle exhaust using equivalent-electron counting rather than a local wall flux density.

The global removal rate is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}} = \frac{dN_{e,\mathrm{removed}}}{dt}
$$

where $\Gamma_{e,\mathrm{pump}}$ is the pumped particle-removal rate expressed in equivalent electrons, $N_{e,\mathrm{removed}}$ is the cumulative number of electron equivalents removed by wall pumping, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is aggregated over the wall and represents the total pumping throughput for the electron-equivalent population. The electron-equivalent basis does not assert that all removed particles are physical electrons, and the quantity is not an areal flux density, an electrical current, or a rate for one specified neutral species.

It is the electron-specific specialization of the general [particle-removal flux at the wall due to pumping](name:particle_rate_at_wall_due_to_pumping). In contrast, [neutral particle flux at the wall due to pumping](name:neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_pumping) uses a specified neutral species as its counting population rather than equivalent-electron counting.

This is an injected electron-equivalent particle flux instead of a pumped one.

rows.name: contradicts-296
rows.planted_sentence: Power inside the flux surface is only the local absorbed power density at that surface.

item.documentation:
Cumulative absorbed electromagnetic-wave power deposited in the plasma volume enclosed by a selected magnetic flux surface. It includes absorption by electron, ion, and fast populations and represents an enclosed quantity rather than a local power density.

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{abs}}(\psi) = \int_{V(\psi)} p_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{abs}}(\psi)$ is the cumulative absorbed wave power, $\psi$ is the label of the selected magnetic flux surface, $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by that surface, $p_{\mathrm{abs}}^{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total absorbed wave power density at spatial position $\mathbf{x}$ summed over electrons, ions, and fast populations, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

This quantity is cumulative over the enclosed volume and is not a local deposition density or a population-resolved contribution. Population-specific quantities such as [thermal electron power at an inside flux surface](name:thermal_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface) and [thermal ion power at an inside flux surface](name:thermal_ion_power_at_inside_flux_surface) resolve components of this aggregate. When the selected surface encloses the full absorbing plasma volume, it equals [total absorbed wave power](name:total_absorbed_wave_power).

Power inside the flux surface is only the local absorbed power density at that surface.

item.documentation:
Fast electron absorbed wave power is the total coherent-wave power transferred to the fast, non-thermal electron population throughout the plasma volume. It is the fast-electron component of [electron absorbed wave power](name:electron_absorbed_wave_power).

The volume-integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-electron absorbed wave power, $p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local coherent-wave power density absorbed by fast electrons at position $\mathbf{x}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

This quantity excludes wave power absorbed by bulk thermal electrons, ions, and other populations, as well as wave power that is launched but not absorbed. Unlike [fast electron power at inside flux surface](name:fast_electron_power_at_inside_flux_surface), it represents the total plasma-volume integral rather than a cumulative value inside a specified flux surface. The population scope is complementary to [thermal electron absorbed wave power](name:thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power).

In a wave-heating power balance, this value can be grouped with the absorbed powers of thermal electrons and ions.

item.documentation:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. For this reference quantity, the designated location is the radius at which the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified, making it the reference specialization of major_radius.

At the designated reference location, the major radius is defined geometrically by:

$$
R_0 = \sqrt{X_0^2 + Y_0^2}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $X_0$ and $Y_0$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the reference location perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis. The Cartesian basis is right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$; the corresponding cylindrical frame is right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). It is not a pointwise plasma-radius field, a flux-surface average, or a region integral, and it has no species or plasma-population scope.

Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference radius. It is also distinct from a [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) assigned to an arbitrary geometric point or measurement location.

The reference radius and the vacuum toroidal magnetic field form the reference pair $R_0$ and $B_0$, where $B_0$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic field specified at the reference radius. Their product $R_0B_0$ supplies the geometric-field scale used in normalized toroidal-flux and current-density definitions.

In an axisymmetric current-free region, vacuum toroidal-field strength at another major radius scales inversely with that radius.

item.documentation:
Poloidal beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of the total pressure content of the confined plasma relative to the magnetic-pressure scale generated by the plasma current. It characterizes pressure relative to the poloidal magnetic field rather than the toroidal magnetic field.

The defining relation is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{R_0\,\mu_0\,I_p^2}
$$

where $\beta_p$ is poloidal beta, $p$ is the total plasma pressure, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current.

The pressure integral extends over the entire confined plasma volume and aggregates the pressure of all included plasma populations, so this quantity is global rather than local or species-resolved. It excludes any separate normalization based on minor radius or reference toroidal magnetic-field strength.

As the poloidal-field member of the [beta](name:beta) family, poloidal beta uses a current- and major-radius-based poloidal magnetic-pressure scale. It is distinct from [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta), which normalizes pressure to a toroidal magnetic-field scale, and from normalized_toroidal_plasma_beta, which applies an additional engineering normalization.

item.documentation:
Coolant mass flow rate is the rate of coolant mass crossing a reference section of a fluid-flow path. It represents fluid throughput for cooling loops and plant-component ports without selecting one particular physical location.

The defining mass flow rate is

$$
\dot{m} = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m$ is the coolant mass crossing the reference section, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate coolant stream and is not a volumetric flow rate, coolant temperature, transit time, or thermal power. The enthalpy transport associated with the flow is $\dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the specific enthalpies of the coolant at the outlet and inlet; the [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) helps characterize the outlet state. The [coolant transit time of a plant component port](name:coolant_transit_time_of_plant_component_port) is a related elapsed-time quantity, not part of the mass flow rate itself.

Sign convention: Positive when coolant crosses the reference section in the designated positive flow direction from inlet toward outlet.

item.documentation:
Toroidal coordinate of a neutron detector is the angular coordinate of the detector's geometric center about the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$. Here $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical-height coordinate.

For a detector center whose projection onto the plane perpendicular to $\hat{Z}$ has Cartesian coordinates $x_c$ and $y_c$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and $\phi=0$ along $+\hat{x}$, the toroidal coordinate is

$$

$$

where $\phi_\mathrm{n}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the neutron detector, and $x_c$ and $y_c$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the detector geometric center projected onto the plane perpendicular to $\hat{Z}$.

This quantity applies specifically to a neutron detector and to the point representing its geometric center. The aggregation convention is none: it denotes one detector center, not an average, sum, or representative angle over several detectors; it is geometrically undefined for a center on the symmetry axis, where no toroidal direction is selected.

It is not a detector orientation, angular extent, line-of-sight direction, or the toroidal coordinate of an aperture or other component. It specializes the generic [toroidal coordinate of a detector](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_detector) to neutron detectors and is distinct from [toroidal coordinate of an aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture), which refers to an aperture's own geometric center.

Sign convention: Positive when the detector geometric center is displaced in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

The radial volumetric force is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. $$

item.documentation:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions rather than representing only one pressure population.

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only, and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$ defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure integral.

rows.name: says_nothing-362
rows.planted_sentence: Varying this coefficient in a neutral-transport model can test the sensitivity of predicted energy losses to the closure.

item.documentation:
This coefficient specifies the strength of the limiter applied to energy transport by neutral particles occupying one selected internal state. It is a closure parameter rather than an energy flux or an energy density.

The limiter imposes the bound

$$
\lvert \mathbf{q}_E \rvert \leq \alpha_E q_{E,\max}
$$

where $\alpha_E$ is this flux-limiter coefficient, $\mathbf{q}_E$ is the energy-flux-density vector carried by the selected neutral internal state, and $q_{E,\max}$ is the prescribed maximum admissible magnitude for that energy flux.

The coefficient applies to the energy channel of neutral transport for the specified internal state. It does not sum over neutral internal states or neutral species, does not represent the energy flux itself, and has no edge-region restriction in its definition. It is distinct from the corresponding momentum limiter, such as the [neutral internal-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient_over_edge_region), which constrains momentum rather than energy transport.

The coefficient scales the admissible energy-flux bound in the closure: increasing $\alpha_E$ permits a larger maximum energy flux relative to $q_{E,\max}$, while the coefficient itself remains a dimensionless scalar.

Varying this coefficient in a neutral-transport model can test the sensitivity of predicted energy losses to the closure.

rows.name: says_nothing-411
rows.planted_sentence: Tracking this rate beside the co-passing rate can show how thermal-particle source contributions differ between the two passing-orbit classes.

item.documentation:
Counter-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the counter-passing orbit class. Counter-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction.

The source contribution to the evolution of the counter-passing thermal particle number density is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)=\left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{source}}
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is this source rate, $n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged number density of counter-passing thermal particles, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $t$ is time, and the source subscript denotes the explicit particle-source contribution. Positive values represent net particle addition, while negative values represent net particle removal.

This quantity applies only to the thermal population in the counter-passing orbit class and is averaged over magnetic flux surfaces. It is not summed over co-passing or trapped orbit classes and excludes nonthermal particle populations. The corresponding [co-passing thermal particle source rate](name:co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) applies the same source definition to the co-passing orbit class.

The broader [thermal particle source rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate) aggregates the orbit-population contributions, including this counter-passing component; this quantity therefore represents only the counter-passing contribution rather than the total thermal source.

Tracking this rate beside the co-passing rate can show how thermal-particle source contributions differ between the two passing-orbit classes.

Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. This quantity is a single designated geometric reference value associated with the vacuum toroidal magnetic field, represented by [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). Unlike [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius), which averages the radius over a nested magnetic flux surface, this quantity identifies one reference radius. item.documentation:
Coolant mass flow rate is the rate of coolant mass crossing a reference section of a fluid-flow path. It represents fluid throughput for cooling loops and plant-component ports without selecting one particular physical location.

The defining mass flow rate is

$$
\dot{m} = \frac{\mathrm{d}m}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $\dot{m}$ is the coolant mass flow rate, $m$ is the coolant mass crossing the reference section, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the aggregate coolant stream and is not a volumetric flow rate, coolant temperature, transit time, or thermal power. The enthalpy transport associated with the flow is $\dot{m}(h_{\mathrm{out}}-h_{\mathrm{in}})$, where $h_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $h_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the specific enthalpies of the coolant at the outlet and inlet; the [coolant temperature at outlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_outlet) helps characterize the outlet state. The radial volumetric force is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. item.documentation:
The ordinary-mode power fraction quantifies the share of one launched electron-cyclotron beam carried by the ordinary (O) polarization mode rather than the extraordinary (X) mode.

It is defined by the ratio

$$
f_O = \frac{P_O}{P_{\mathrm{EC}}}
$$

where $f_O$ is the ordinary-mode power fraction, $P_O$ is the launched power in the ordinary mode, and $P_{\mathrm{EC}}$ is the total launched power of the electron-cyclotron beam.

The quantity applies to a single electron-cyclotron beam and uses launched beam power aggregated over the beam's ordinary-mode content. It excludes power from other beams and does not represent the total launched power itself. Values of $f_O=1$ and $f_O=0$ denote pure ordinary-mode and pure extraordinary-mode launch, respectively.

This power partition is distinct from [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam), which describes the shape and handedness of a polarization ellipse rather than the O-mode fraction of an electron-cyclotron beam.

item.documentation:
MHD plasma stored energy is the global energy content assigned to the plasma by integrating its equilibrium-reconstructed total kinetic pressure over the full plasma volume. It includes thermal and fast-particle contributions rather than representing only one pressure population.

The defining relation is

$$
W_{\mathrm{MHD}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_{\mathrm{plasma}}} p_{\mathrm{tot}}\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{MHD}}$ is the MHD plasma stored energy, $p_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total kinetic pressure determined by the equilibrium reconstruction, $V_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ is the complete plasma volume, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

This is a global volume-integrated quantity over all included plasma populations. It is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which integrates thermal pressure only, and from [diamagnetic energy](name:diamagnetic_energy), which is restricted to pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The factor $3/2$ defines the stored-energy convention used for the total kinetic-pressure integral.

The time derivative of this stored energy can be compared with net heating power in a plasma energy balance.

rows.name: says_nothing-362
rows.planted_sentence: Varying this coefficient in a neutral-transport model can test the sensitivity of predicted energy losses to the closure.

item.documentation:
This coefficient specifies the strength of the limiter applied to energy transport by neutral particles occupying one selected internal state. It is a closure parameter rather than an energy flux or an energy density.

The limiter imposes the bound

$$
\lvert \mathbf{q}_E \rvert \leq \alpha_E q_{E,\max}
$$

where $\alpha_E$ is this flux-limiter coefficient, $\mathbf{q}_E$ is the energy-flux-density vector carried by the selected neutral internal state, and $q_{E,\max}$ is the prescribed maximum admissible magnitude for that energy flux.

The coefficient applies to the energy channel of neutral transport for the specified internal state. It does not sum over neutral internal states or neutral species, does not represent the energy flux itself, and has no edge-region restriction in its definition. It is distinct from the corresponding momentum limiter, such as the [neutral internal-state momentum flux-limiter coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_momentum_flux_limiter_coefficient_over_edge_region), which constrains momentum rather than energy transport.

The coefficient scales the admissible energy-flux bound in the closure: increasing $\alpha_E$ permits a larger maximum energy flux relative to $q_{E,\max}$, while the coefficient itself remains a dimensionless scalar.

Varying this coefficient in a neutral-transport model can test the sensitivity of predicted energy losses to the closure.

rows.name: says_nothing-49
rows.planted_sentence: Comparing this aggregate with species-resolved ion temperatures can reveal ion populations that are not in thermal equilibrium.

item.documentation:
Ion average temperature is the effective kinetic temperature of the combined ion population, formed from all included ion species and their charge states at a given plasma location.

The density-weighted mean is defined by

$$
T_i = \frac{\sum_s \sum_z n_{s,z} T_{s,z}}{\sum_s \sum_z n_{s,z}}
$$

where $T_i$ is the ion average temperature, $s$ indexes the included ion species, $z$ indexes the charge states of each species, $n_{s,z}$ is the number density of that species and charge state, and $T_{s,z}$ is its temperature.

The aggregation includes all ion species and all charge states, with number-density weighting rather than an unweighted arithmetic mean. The quantity applies throughout the closed-field plasma and scrape-off layer. For radial evaluations, closed-field values use flux-surface averaging, while scrape-off-layer values use the local outboard-midplane value.

This quantity excludes neutral particles and electrons, is not a sum of temperatures or an energy density, and does not itself denote a volume, line, or spatial average. The spatial evaluation convention is distinct from the intrinsic species and charge-state aggregation.

The combined-population interpretation corresponds to [total ion temperature](name:total_ion_temperature); [volume-averaged total ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature) additionally applies a spatial volume average.

Comparing this aggregate with species-resolved ion temperatures can reveal ion populations that are not in thermal equilibrium.

rows.name: says_nothing-411
rows.planted_sentence: Tracking this rate beside the co-passing rate can show how thermal-particle source contributions differ between the two passing-orbit classes.

item.documentation:
Counter-passing thermal particle source rate is the flux-surface-averaged volumetric rate at which thermal particles enter or leave the counter-passing orbit class. Counter-passing particles are passing particles whose guiding-center toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction.

The source contribution to the evolution of the counter-passing thermal particle number density is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)=\left.\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}(\psi,t)}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{source}}
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is this source rate, $n_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged number density of counter-passing thermal particles, $\psi$ is the magnetic flux-surface label, $t$ is time, and the source subscript denotes the explicit particle-source contribution. Positive values represent net particle addition, while negative values represent net particle removal.

This quantity applies only to the thermal population in the counter-passing orbit class and is averaged over magnetic flux surfaces. It is not summed over co-passing or trapped orbit classes and excludes nonthermal particle populations. The corresponding [co-passing thermal particle source rate](name:co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate) applies the same source definition to the co-passing orbit class.

The broader [thermal particle source rate](name:thermal_particle_source_rate) aggregates the orbit-population contributions, including this counter-passing component; this quantity therefore represents only the counter-passing contribution rather than the total thermal source.

Tracking this rate beside the co-passing rate can show how thermal-particle source contributions differ between the two passing-orbit classes.
